doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Bobby Short as orchestrator-pianist; meeting Len Garment
summary: Short's gift for Strayhorn-like orchestration and counterpoint; a thousand shows, and Teddy Wilson's thumb remark.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: a great pianist. People said oh he rushed or he didn’t have a jazz feel. Who cares what he did. He was a brilliant orchestrator. Monk you would love this. He could sit down, like you could ask him to play a tune he hadn’t played in thirty years. He’d sit down and he’d play and he’d find his key, and what would come out of the piano would sound like a Billy Strayhorn arrangement. I mean he spontaneously could do that. I mean and he loved Ellington I mean that was his whole life was Ivy Anderson and Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn. He grew up with it. He knew them. He knew Ivy Anderson. And he could just create these things, I mean amazing. I would sit sometimes at the Carlyle and we’d be playing an arr — okay so what would happen was eventually Mark Loepman and James began to realize — because I would go to Bobby’s house and record him playing and we would talk about the key and the tempo and what he wanted and then we’d arrange — and I’d record it and I’d give a copy of the recording to Mark or to James. And they started telling me you know what? Everything in the arrangement is in the piano. See I was adding things. You don’t need to add anything. Orchestrate the piano and you can add a few notes but that’s the arrangement. You couldn’t come up with something better. So we started playing these arrangements at the Carlyle and I’m sitting like this and Bobby, I’m sitting on a banquette, and Bobby is facing that way at the piano. I’m facing him. And I’m watching him. We wound up doing a — I wound up doing a thousand one- hour shows with him. It was 20 weeks a year for five years. So that’s — anyway it was 1000 shows because there were two shows a night. And he started playing on the piano counterpoint to the arrangement that was written of his piano playing, and he could, Monk, he could create two and three levels of counterpoint at the piano. It was not comping like a D flat 7, C minor, it was counterpoint. And he had like this pearly upper register and then he had like this middle thing, and then he had these strange bass notes. And I’d be listening, when I wasn’t playing. I thought Jesus, what is he doing? He’s spontaneously has three lines. It’s almost like the way that Teddy Wilson played with the Benny Goodman trio and quartet. And Teddy Wilson’s son once said to me, he said, “You know Benny Goodman should have paid my father triple scale.” And I said why? “Because he has three things going on at the piano. He has a left hand, he has a right hand, and he has his thumb.” There’s three levels of stuff going on. Well anyway, now, so I had all that stuff was going on and that was this incredibly rich part of my life, I mean rich in terms of experience. And it was really great, it was really too much, but I was handling it, I was in my early 40s. Through the Smithsonian Jazz Orchestra and one of the lesser bands I played in I got to know a wonderful classical clarinetist in New York named Paul Garment. And Paul’s father was Len Garment, Leonard Garment. And I knew who Len Garment was because he was a fascinating guy, I mean he was known for being counsel to the president during Watergate.
